passages.title: Abundance given, worship owed, the reviler cut off
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

Three short ayat, revealed as an answer. Enemies of the Prophet ﷺ had said that he was *abtar* — cut off, a man with no male offspring to carry his name, whose memory would end with his death. Allah replies by naming what He has actually given him (ayah 1), telling him how to respond to such a gift (ayah 2), and turning the insult back on the one who hurled it (ayah 3). The unity of the passage is that single movement: **gift, gratitude, verdict.**

Ibn Kathir reads the second ayah as flowing straight out of the first: *just as We have given you the abundant goodness in this life and the Hereafter — and from that is the river described in the hadith — then make your prayer and your sacrifice solely and sincerely for your Lord.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same connection in terms of thankfulness: ayah 1 gives the glad tiding, and ayah 2 directs the Prophet ﷺ in how to express his gratitude to Allah for it — by prayer, and by sacrifice.

## The taunt behind the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports — from Ibn Abi Hatim on the authority of Suddi, and from Baihaqi in *Dalāʼil un-Nubuwwah* on the authority of Muhammad Ibn Ali Ibn Husain — that the Arabs used to taunt and revile a man who had lost his male children, calling him *abtar*: one with no male offspring. In keeping with this social evil, when the young son of the Prophet ﷺ, Qasim, passed away, some leaders of the Quraysh — especially ʿAs Ibn Waʼil — began telling people that they no longer needed to bother about him, because he had no sons to carry on his name and would be forgotten after his death; he is *abtar*, his lineage cut off. On that occasion the surah was revealed. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Mazhari for this.)

Ibn Kathir gathers the same picture from several angles. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Saʿid bin Jubayr and Qatadah all said the ayah was revealed about al-ʿAs bin Waʼil, who would say whenever the Prophet ﷺ was mentioned, "Leave him — he is a man who is cut off, having no descendants; when he dies he will not be remembered." Shamir bin ʿAtiyah said it was revealed concerning ʿUqbah bin Abi Muʿayt. Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿIkrimah both said it was revealed about Kaʿb bin al-Ashraf and a group of the disbelievers of the Quraysh. It has been reported that ʿAta' said it was about Abu Lahab, who went to the idolaters when a son of the Prophet ﷺ died and announced, "Muhammad has been cut off tonight." As-Suddi explained the social background plainly: when a man's male sons died, people used to say *he has been cut off*, so when the sons of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died they said this of him.

The commentators do not all name the same man, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records this honestly: most narratives identify the reviler as ʿAs Ibn Waʼil, others as ʿUqbah, and yet others as Kaʿb Ibn Ashraf. The insult was in the air; more than one mouth carried it.

There is a second occasion recorded by al-Bazzar from Ibn ʿAbbas, whose chain of narration Ibn Kathir states is authentic. Kaʿb bin al-Ashraf — whom Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies as a Jew of Madinah — came to Makkah, and the Quraysh said to him: "You are the leader of the people. What do you think about this worthless man who is cut off from his people? He claims that he is better than us, while we are the people of the place of pilgrimage, the people of custodianship of the Kaʿbah, and the people who supply water to the pilgrims." Kaʿb answered, "You all are better than him." So Allah revealed: *Only the one who hates you is truly cut off.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Mazhari says Muslim also transmitted this incident.

Notice what was really at stake. The Quraysh were not arguing theology; they were counting assets — sons, the office of custodianship, the honour of supplying the pilgrims with water. Against that ledger they set one man who had lost his boys. Allah's reply does not dispute the accounting. It changes the currency.

## Ayah 1: what *al-Kawthar* means

**"Indeed, We have granted you abundant goodness."**

Al-Bukhari records from Saʿid bin Jubayr that Ibn ʿAbbas said of *al-Kawthar*: "It is the good which Allah gave to him." Al-Bukhari also records from Saʿid bin Jubayr that Ibn ʿAbbas said, "*Al-Kawthar* is the abundant goodness." Ibn Kathir explains why the word carries that weight: it comes from the word *kathrah* (abundance), and *al-Kawthar* linguistically means an abundance of goodness — so from this goodness is the river in Paradise.

There is a small, instructive exchange here. Abu Bishr said to Saʿid bin Jubayr, "People are claiming that it is a river in Paradise." Saʿid replied, "The river which is in Paradise is *part of* the goodness which Allah gave him." That is the reconciliation both commentaries adopt: the word is broad, the river is included. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Mujahid therefore interprets it as the abundant goodness of this world as well as the next, and Ibn Kathir concludes that the explanation "abundant goodness" includes the river and other things as well.

**The surah's own commentary.** Muslim, Abu Dawud and an-Nasaʼi record from Anas: "While we were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the Masjid, he dozed off into a slumber. Then he lifted his head smiling. We said, 'O Messenger of Allah, what has caused you to laugh?' He said, *Verily, a Surah was just revealed to me* — and he recited [this surah]. Then he said, *Do you all know what al-Kawthar is?* We said, 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: *Verily, it is a river that my Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, has promised me, and it has abundant goodness. It is a pond where my Ummah will be brought to on the Day of Judgement. Its containers are as numerous as the stars in the sky. Then a servant of Allah from among them will be prevented from it, and I will say: "O Lord, verily he is from my Ummah." Then He will say: "Verily, you do not know what he introduced after you."*" This is the wording of Muslim. Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad also recorded this hadith from Muhammad bin Fudayl, from al-Mukhtar bin Fulful, from Anas bin Malik; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records it as being in Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud and Nasaʼi.

Sit with the smile. The insult was public and it stung — and the answer Allah sent left His Messenger ﷺ lifting his head smiling.

**Descriptions of the river.** Al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih, and so did Muslim, from Anas that when the Prophet ﷺ was taken up to the heaven he said: *I came to a river whose banks had domes of hollowed pearl. I said, "O Jibril, what is this?" He replied, "This is al-Kawthar."* That is the wording of al-Bukhari. Imam Ahmad records from Anas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *I entered Paradise and I came to a river whose banks had tents made of pearls. So I thrust my hand into its flowing water and found that it was the strongest smell of musk. So I asked, "O Jibril, what is this?" He replied, "This is al-Kawthar which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has given you."* Ahmad also records from Anas that when a man asked what al-Kawthar was, he ﷺ replied: *It is a river in Paradise which my Lord has given me. It is whiter than milk and sweeter than honey. There are birds in it whose necks are long like carrots.* ʿUmar said, "O Messenger of Allah, verily they will be beautiful!" The Prophet ﷺ replied, *The one who eats them will be more beautiful than them, O ʿUmar.* And Imam Ahmad records from Ibn ʿUmar that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *Al-Kawthar is a river in Paradise whose banks are of gold and it runs over pearls. Its water is whiter than milk and sweeter than honey* — recorded in this manner also by at-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir, and at-Tirmidhi said, "*Hasan Sahih*." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān remarks of such traditions, describing the cleanness and sweetness of the water and the pearls adorning its banks, that these qualities cannot be compared with anything in this world.

**The river and the fountain.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out five points from the hadith of Anas, and two are worth pausing on. First: the actual river of Kawthar is in Paradise, while the fountain of Kawthar will be on the Plain of Gathering — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Ibn Kathir that two channels will lead from the sky to supply that fountain with the water of Kawthar, and that it will have more cups than the stars in the sky. This reconciles the narratives telling us that believers arrive at the fountain *before* their entry into Paradise. Second, as for those turned away: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains them as people who later turned away from Islam, or who were not Muslims at all but expressed their Islam only hypocritically, their hypocrisy exposed after the Prophet ﷺ — and then adds, as a scholar should, "Allah knows best."

## Ayah 2: the worship this gift asks for

**"So pray and sacrifice to your Lord alone."**

Ibn Kathir reads the connection directly: just as We have given you the abundant goodness in this life and the Hereafter — and from that is the river described above — then make your obligatory and optional prayer, and your sacrifice of animals, solely and sincerely for your Lord. Worship Him alone and do not associate any partner with Him; and sacrifice pronouncing His Name alone, without ascribing any partner to Him. He cites Allah's words: *"Say: Verily, my Salah, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, the Lord of all that exists. He has no partner. And of this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims"* (6:162–163), and *"And do not eat from what Allah's Name has not been pronounced over; indeed that is Fisq"* (6:121).

Ibn Kathir adds that this is the opposite of the way of the idolaters — prostrating to other than Allah, and sacrificing in other than His Name. The act is not what separates the believer from them. The One it is offered to is.

**The word *wanḥar*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the imperative is derived from *naḥr*, which means to sacrifice by stabbing upwards into the jugular vein — the way of slaughter for camels, as opposed to other cattle. Because the Arabs generally used to sacrifice camels, the verse employs this imperative; occasionally the word *naḥr* is used in the general sense of "sacrifice." Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAta', Mujahid, ʿIkrimah and al-Hasan all said, "This means with this the *Budn* should be sacrificed," and that Qatadah, Muhammad bin Kaʿb al-Qurazi, ad-Dahhak, ar-Rabiʿ, ʿAta' al-Khurasani, al-Hakam, Ismaʿil bin Abi Khalid and others from the Salaf have all said the same. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same from Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAta', Mujahid and Hasan Basri: *wanḥar* means to sacrifice, to offer oblation.

**Where views differ.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān mentions that some people have attributed to certain leading exegetes the view that this imperative means "fold your hands or arms on the chest." It also records Ibn Kathir's judgement that such narrations are *munkar* — a term it defines for us as a narration transmitted by a weak narrator that contradicts the narration of a stronger and more reliable authority. The weight of the transmitted commentary, in both books, is on sacrifice.

**Why these two acts.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point beautifully: salah is the highest form of physical worship, and sacrifice the highest form of monetary worship. Together they cover a person entirely — what you do with your body and what you do with your property. And sacrifice in the name of Allah is itself a fight against idolatry, because the idolaters used to sacrifice in the names of their idols; on that basis, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, the Islamic sacrifice is distinctive and important.

## Ayah 3: who is really cut off

**"Only the one who hates you is truly cut off."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word *shāniʼ* is derived from *shaʼn* and means "one who hates, traducer, insulter." Ibn Kathir expands the object of that hatred: indeed he who hates you, O Muhammad, and hates what you have come with of guidance, truth, clear proof and manifest light — *he* is the most cut off, the meanest, the lowliest person, who will not be remembered.

Read the ayah against the taunt and see how exactly it answers. They said *he* is cut off. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the reply: on the one hand the enemy has been rebutted, and on the other their argument has been rebuffed — it is not the Prophet ﷺ, but his enemies, who are *abtar*, cut off. The word they threw did land — but not where they aimed it.

**The reply to their arithmetic.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers on two levels. First, Allah granted His Messenger ﷺ al-Kawthar, abundant goodness which includes a multitude of children: there is no scarcity of his lineal children, and his lineal offspring will remain till the Day of Judgement, though from his daughters. Second, and greater: a Prophet is the spiritual father of his entire Ummah, and the Prophet ﷺ is the spiritual father of his whole Ummah till the end of time. He will therefore have the largest number of spiritual children compared with the Ummahs of the Prophets who came before him — sons, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, far more faithful, obedient and loving than the sons of any father.

## The verdict of history

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with an observation any reader can verify. Imagine how Allah has raised the name of His Messenger ﷺ and exalted his reputation in every nook and corner of the world, from the inception of his prophethood until today — his blessed name recited along with Allah's Name five times a day from the minarets — and it will continue to be so until the end of time. In the Hereafter he will be granted *al-Maqām al-Maḥmūd*, the Praised Station, where he will make the Grand Intercession on behalf of the entire progeny of Adam.

Then it asks: where are the children of ʿAs Ibn Waʼil? Where are the children of Kaʿb Ibn Ashraf? Where are the children of ʿUqbah, and what happened to their families? Their very own names have been lost to the world. No one cares to remember them. Those who thought that the Prophet ﷺ would soon become unknown have themselves become unknown; their names have been preserved in Islamic traditions only for purposes of interpreting the relevant verses. Ibn Kathir says the same: they thought in their ignorance that if his sons died his remembrance would be cut off — Allah forbid! To the contrary, Allah preserved his remembrance for all the world to see, and obligated all the servants to follow his Law, and this will continue for all of time until the Day of Gathering and the coming of the Hereafter.

*"So, O people of insight, take note!"* (59:2)

## Living it

**Measure yourself in the right currency.** The Quraysh counted sons, custodianship and the honour of watering the pilgrims, and by that reckoning they won the argument in their own eyes. Allah's answer was not a better score in their game but a different accounting altogether. What is granted here is abundant goodness — and Ibn ʿAbbas' reading, as Ibn Kathir explains it, keeps that deliberately wide: it includes the river of Paradise and other things as well.

**Let gratitude become worship, not just feeling.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 2 exactly this way — as the direction given to the Prophet ﷺ for expressing gratitude for the glad tiding of ayah 1. The thankfulness of this surah does not stop at relief; it turns immediately into prayer and sacrifice, body and wealth both given back.

**Guard the direction.** *To your Lord alone.* Ibn Kathir's whole reading of ayah 2 is about sincerity: prayer and sacrifice belong to Allah alone, worshipping Him without partner, with His Name alone pronounced over the slaughter.

**Fear the small breach more than the loud enemy.** The most sobering line in this passage is not about the revilers. It is the servant prevented from the fountain while the Prophet ﷺ says, *O Lord, verily he is from my Ummah* — and the answer comes, *you do not know what he introduced after you.* The enemies of ayah 3 were never the real danger to a believer's share of Kawthar.

**Take the long view when you are belittled.** The surah's own history is its argument, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān invites us to check it against world history. Insults that seemed decisive at the time have been outlived, and the revelation that made the Prophet ﷺ lift his head smiling is still being recited by his spiritual children.

May the blessings of Allah and His peace be upon him forever until the Day of Assembling.
